title: Rain and dew
hookLine: a seasonal line asks for rain in winter and dew in summer

lines: WE NOTICE WEATHER WHEN IT'S IN THE WAY.
cards: Most of us notice the weather only when it's in the way. Rain on the commute, heat on the walk to the car. In the land of Israel, two thousand years ago, rain was not an inconvenience.
It was the whole year. There was no river to irrigate from, like Egypt's Nile. Winter rain came or it didn't, and with it came the harvest, or hunger.
So the prayer book did something unusual. It put the weather inside the Amidah, and it gave it a season.

teach.h: WHO MAKES THE WIND BLOW, THE RAIN FALL.
teach.b: In the middle of Gevurot, the blessing of God's might, a short line comes and goes. From the end of Sukkot in the autumn until Passover in the spring, people add: mashiv haruach umorid hagashem.
Who makes the wind blow and the rain fall. At Passover, the line stops.

teach.h: IN SUMMER: WHO MAKES THE DEW FALL.
teach.b: In summer, many communities, Sephardi Jews and Ashkenazi Jews in Israel among them, say instead: morid hatal, who makes the dew fall.
Many Ashkenazi communities outside Israel say nothing about weather in the summer months. Why put rain in a blessing about God's might?

The Mishnah, at the opening of tractate Taanit, calls it gevurot geshamim, the mighty deeds of rain. Rain sits next to reviving the dead because both bring life back to something that looked finished.
A field after a dry summer, the rabbis are saying, is a small resurrection. And why dew in summer?
The Talmud notes that dew is never withheld; it comes every night, quietly, even in the driest months. So the summer line isn't a request for something rare. It's noticing something faithful.
You heard the rain promise in the Shema's second paragraph.
In the old Jewish translation: "I will give the rain of your land in its season." Not all the time. The right weather at the right time.
Twice a year, at Sukkot and at Passover, the whole community changes one line together, and the prayer turns with the earth.

how: From Shemini Atzeret at the end of Sukkot until the first day of Passover, Jews add mashiv haruach umorid hagashem to the Amidah's second blessing; in summer many Sephardi communities and Ashkenazim in Israel say morid hatal, while many Ashkenazim outside Israel add nothing.

games.q: you're arranging the Amidah. where should a line about rain go?
o: in the blessing about the ancestors.
in the blessing of God's might, next to reviving the dead.
games.why: the rabbis call rain a mighty deed. like reviving the dead, it brings life back to what looked finished.

practice: Look out a window, or remember the last time you were outside: rain, sun, wind, gray, frost. Then think about what that weather is doing for something else, the soil, a tree, a reservoir somewhere, a farmer's field.
Let it be, for a minute, not in your way but on its way somewhere.
